stem: You need to gather data from three independent sources whose results don't depend on each other, and latency matters. Which orchestration pattern fits?

options.label: A
options.body: Parallel — fan out the independent subtasks, then fan in the results.
options.rationale: Correct. Parallel orchestration is for independent subtasks where latency matters; they share no state.

options.label: B
options.body: Sequential — A → B → C, each passing its result forward.
options.rationale: Sequential is for when each step needs the previous step's output — not the case here, and it's slower.

options.label: C
options.body: Pipeline — an assembly line of specialized stages.
options.rationale: Pipeline chains stages where each output feeds the next; these tasks are independent, not staged.

options.label: D
options.body: Dynamic adaptive — let the model decide the decomposition at runtime.
options.rationale: Dynamic adaptive is for tasks whose structure is unknown upfront; here the decomposition is already known.

stem: A task's structure can't be predicted at design time — its complexity and the right decomposition only become clear as work proceeds. Which orchestration approach?

options.label: A
options.body: Dynamic adaptive — the model decides the decomposition at runtime.
options.rationale: Correct. When you can't predict the structure upfront, let the coordinator reason about decomposition at runtime.

options.label: B
options.body: A fixed sequential pipeline defined upfront.
options.rationale: A fixed pipeline assumes you know the stages — you don't, so it locks you into the wrong structure.

options.label: C
options.body: Parallel fan-out across a preset list of subtasks.
options.rationale: Preset parallel subtasks require knowing the decomposition in advance.

options.label: D
options.body: A hardcoded decision tree mapping inputs to steps.
options.rationale: Decision trees are the opposite of adaptive — they break on cases they weren't designed for.

stem: How many tools should a single specialized subagent be scoped to, per the guide's design guidance?

options.label: A
options.body: About 4–5 tools maximum — focused sets reduce selection errors.
options.rationale: Correct. Scope each agent to ~4–5 tools; the guide's over-tooling example is 18 instead of 4–5.

options.label: B
options.body: As many as possible, so one agent can handle anything.
options.rationale: One agent with many tools increases selection errors — the anti-pattern.

options.label: C
options.body: Exactly one single tool per agent in every case, regardless of the agent's role or the task it handles.
options.rationale: Too rigid; ~4–5 related tools per role is the guidance, not exactly one.

options.label: D
options.body: Around 10 to 12 tools per agent, chosen to balance capability breadth against keeping the agent focused.
options.rationale: Still too many; the guidance is ~4–5 per agent.

stem: When an agent escalates to a human who can't see the conversation, which structured handoff format does the exam expect?

options.label: A
options.body: Customer ID, a factual summary of what happened, the root cause, and the recommended action.
options.rationale: Correct. The four-field structured handoff (who, what, why, suggested next step) lets the human pick up instantly without re-investigating.

options.label: B
options.body: The full raw conversation transcript, handed over for the human agent to read through in its entirety themselves.
options.rationale: Dumping the transcript forces the human to re-do the investigation.

options.label: C
options.body: Just the customer's original opening message together with a reference ID for the human to look the case up by.
options.rationale: Drops the tool-derived context and diagnosis the agent already produced.

options.label: D
options.body: A generic error message that simply signals to the human that they now need to take the case over from the agent.
options.rationale: Never silently fail with a generic error — produce a structured handoff.

stem: Mid-task, the model starts repeating itself, contradicting earlier statements, and ignoring recent tool results. What's the right fix?

options.label: A
options.body: Fresh start with an injected curated summary of the important facts.
options.rationale: Correct. Those are stale-context signals. The fix isn't 'more context' — it's a fresh conversation seeded with extracted facts.

options.label: B
options.body: Add more context to remind the model of what it said.
options.rationale: Piling on more context into an already-stale window makes it worse, not better.

options.label: C
options.body: Increase the iteration cap so it has more turns.
options.rationale: Iteration caps don't address stale/polluted context.

options.label: D
options.body: Lower the temperature to make it more consistent.
options.rationale: Temperature doesn't fix a context window that's full or stale.

stem: You want to explore two divergent implementation approaches from the same analyzed baseline without either polluting the other's context. Which mechanism?

options.label: A
options.body: fork_session — branch from the shared baseline so each approach has independent context.
options.rationale: Correct. Forking gives each branch the exact baseline with no cross-contamination — ideal for divergent exploration.

options.label: B
options.body: Use --resume on the same session and explore both implementation approaches one after another in sequence.
options.rationale: One thread lets the first approach's reasoning bias the second.

options.label: C
options.body: Start two fresh sessions that each independently re-read all of the baseline files before exploring their approach.
options.rationale: Burns tokens redoing analysis and risks divergent conclusions from the same code.

options.label: D
options.body: Export a summary of the analyzed baseline and start each approach over again from that summary instead.
options.rationale: A summary is lossier than the live baseline state; forking preserves it exactly.

stem: After a tool executes in an agentic loop, what must happen before the next model call so the agent can reason about the result?

options.label: A
options.body: The tool result is appended to the conversation history, then the updated conversation is sent back.
options.rationale: Correct. Tool results must be appended to history so the model can incorporate them on the next iteration.

options.label: B
options.body: The tool result replaces the existing conversation history entirely in order to save context space before the next call.
options.rationale: Replacing history discards what the model needs to reason across turns.

options.label: C
options.body: The result is stored server-side and the model automatically fetches it on the next call without it being sent along.
options.rationale: The API is stateless; you must include the result in the messages you send.

options.label: D
options.body: Nothing needs to happen — the model simply remembers the tool outputs on its own between one call and the next.
options.rationale: It doesn't; without appending the result, the model can't reason about it.

stem: An agent's loop terminates prematurely, cutting off useful work. A teammate proposes 'raise the iteration cap from 10 to 25' to fix it. Is that right?

options.label: A
options.body: No — premature termination is a stop_reason handling bug; iteration caps are only a safety net, not the loop's primary control.
options.rationale: Correct. Fix the stop_reason check (continue on tool_use, stop on end_turn). Caps just bound runaway agents; they don't cause or cure premature stops.

options.label: B
options.body: Yes — raising the iteration cap from 10 up to 25 will always prevent the loop from terminating prematurely on this kind of task.
options.rationale: The cap isn't why it stopped early; the termination logic is. A higher cap masks nothing here.

options.label: C
options.body: Yes, and on top of raising the cap you should also parse the assistant's output text for a phrase like 'done' to know when to stop.
options.rationale: Natural-language parsing is ambiguous — the whole reason stop_reason exists.

options.label: D
options.body: No — instead remove the iteration cap entirely and rely on the response's text length as the signal for when the loop should stop.
options.rationale: Removing the safety net invites runaway loops; text length isn't a termination signal.
